title: Health official warns that future Medicaid cuts could lead to $2.7 billion loss in federal funding
summary: Cuts and changes to Medicaid under the Trump administration could amount to about $2.7 billion in lost federal dollars annually, Maryland health care officials told the Senate Finance Committee Thursday.
content:
by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters January 29, 2026

by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters January 29, 2026

Cuts and changes to Medicaid under the Trump administration could amount to almost $3 billion in lost federal dollars annually, Maryland health care officials told the Senate Finance Committee Thursday.

Much of that loss comes from the anticipated drop in Medicaid coverage due to eligibility changes under HR 1, the federal budget reconciliation bill passed in 2025 known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.”

Deputy Health Secretary Perrie Briskin, in charge of health care financing and state Medicaid director, told senators that “with all provisions implemented” in the bill, the state could lose out on $2.7 billion in federal funding, a loss that would account for almost 20% of current Medicaid funding in the state — numbers that elicited a small gasp from one of the lawmakers on the committee.

“States have tremendous flexibility to shape how the program operates and impacts a broad swath of Marylanders throughout the state,” Briskin said. “The actions you all take can impact care, costs, access, federal compliance — and also open Pandora’s box to other things that are hard to close later.”

Briskin’s comments were part of a what she called a “Medicaid 101” presentation so lawmakers can make budget decisions during the 2026 legislative session on the joint federal-state health care plan that currently covers almost 1.5 million Marylanders.

Just under half of the 1.5 million Marylanders currently enrolled in Medicaid, or 727,800, are under 21 years of age. Almost 239,600 recipients in the state are living with disabilities. Medicaid also covers about 42% of births in the state.

The changes within HR 1 are also expected to result in many Marylanders losing coverage. Just how much is yet to be seen.

Report: Up to 100,000 Marylanders could lose coverage if Medicaid imposes work requirements

The Maryland Department of Health estimates about 15,000 noncitizens could lose coverage when restrictions on which undocumented immigrants can qualify for Medicaid activate this October. That figure is lower than previous estimates of 60,000 undocumented immigrants who could lose coverage.

Another provision from HR 1 adds work requirements for 360,000 Medicaid recipients, which could result in more disenrollments due to the additional administrative burden that will be difficult for struggling Marylanders to keep up with. The department estimates that 115,000 could fall off of Medicaid enrollment due to this requirement.

That same group will also have to prove they are still eligible for Medicaid coverage every six months, which could also contribute to disenrollments — not because they no longer qualify, but because they can’t keep up with the additional administrative hurdles. The additional check-in requirements are also expected to add administrative costs for the state.

The loss in coverage accounts for $1.4 billion of the anticipated drop in federal funding, while the remaining reduction in federal dollars would come from restrictions on how the state funds Medicaid.

The estimated cut of $2.7 billion represents almost 20% of Maryland’s current Medicaid budget of $14.6 billion, leaving Maryland with $11.9 billion in federal and state dollars to cover Medicaid.

Briskin said the Moore administration plans to “invest” in additional staffing and information technology to keep as many people enrolled in Medicaid as possible in the upcoming fiscal year.

The proposed budget for fiscal 2027 would fund Medicaid services at $16.9 billion\, up from $14.6 billion in the current fiscal year. Federal dollars make up most of those costs, with the state contribution in fiscal 2027 coming just under $5.7 billion, up $227 million compared to the current year.

In his proposed budget, Gov. Wes Moore (D) also earmarked $13 million from general funds geared toward implementing the changes under HR 1, to improve administrative operations in hopes of reducing the number of Medicaid recipients who lose coverage needlessly.

“This administration is investing to implement HR 1 in a way that will keep people covered,” Briskin said.

“About $1.4 billion of this $2.7 billion is if that entire 115,000 member group loses coverage,” Briskin said. “But if we can keep most people eligible … then that $2.7 billion could reduce to $1 billion or even much less.”
